statement: In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.
heath_proof: Let ABCD be the given circle; thus it is required to inscribe in the circle ABCD a fifteenangled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular. In the circle ABCD let there be inscribed a side AC of the equilateral triangle inscribed in it, and a side AB of an equilateral pentagon; therefore, of the equal segments of which there are fifteen in the circle ABCD, there will be five in the circumference ABC which is one-third of the circle, and there will be three in the circumference AB which is one-fifth of the circle; therefore in the remainder BC there will be two of the equal segments. Let BC be bisected at E; [III. 30] therefore each of the circumferences BE, EC is a fifteenth of the circle ABCD. If therefore we join BE, EC and fit into the circle ABCD straight lines equal to them and in contiguity, a fifteen-angled figure which is both equilateral and equiangular will have been inscribed in it.
ai_proof_text:
4.16
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given circle. By Proposition 4.2, inscribe an equilateral triangle in the circle, and let one of its sides be the chord subtending the arc AC, so that arc AC is one-third of the whole circumference. By Proposition 4.11, inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon in the same circle, and let one of its sides be the chord subtending the arc AB, so that arc AB is one-fifth of the whole circumference.

**Step 2.** Since arc AC is one-third of the whole circumference and arc AB is one-fifth of the whole circumference, the arc BC, which is the remainder when arc AB is subtracted from arc AC, equals one-third minus one-fifth of the whole circumference, that is, five-fifteenths minus three-fifteenths, which is two-fifteenths of the whole circumference.

**Step 3.** By Proposition 3.30, bisect the arc BC at the point E. Then each of the arcs BE and EC is one-fifteenth of the whole circumference.

**Step 4.** Therefore, if we join BE and EC as straight lines by Postulate 1, each of these chords subtends an arc equal to one-fifteenth of the circumference.

**Step 5.** If we now successively fit into the circle straight lines equal to BE, proceeding around the circumference by Proposition 4.1, we place fifteen equal chords in succession, each subtending one-fifteenth of the circumference.

**Step 6.** By Proposition 3.29, since the fifteen arcs are all equal to one another, the straight lines subtending them are all equal to one another. Therefore the inscribed fifteen-angled figure is equilateral.

**Step 7.** Furthermore, each angle of the inscribed fifteen-angled figure stands on an arc composed of thirteen-fifteenths of the circumference (the whole circumference minus the two arcs on either side of that angle, each being one-fifteenth). Since all the angles of the figure stand on equal arcs, by Proposition 3.27, all the inscribed angles are equal. Therefore the fifteen-angled figure is equiangular.

**Step 8.** Therefore, in the given circle, a fifteen-angled figure has been inscribed which is both equilateral and equiangular. Q.E.F.
